A meeting takes time from multiple people at once, so it should earn that claim. Eyal's answer is to ask what really needs live time, keep the attendee list tighter, and use agendas or written updates so meetings stop becoming default attention sinks.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 15 says meetings become distracting when they are treated as default solutions rather than as costly claims on shared time. A meeting does not take one person's attention. It takes several people's attention at once, often inside the most valuable part of the day.

That is why Eyal says meetings should earn their claim. If the purpose is vague, the agenda is missing, the attendee list is too wide, or the issue could be handled through a written update, then the meeting is not helping enough to justify its cost.

The chapter therefore turns toward design. Ask what decision or coordination actually requires live time. Keep the room smaller. Use shorter windows. Replace status ritual with asynchronous updates where possible. Stop assuming that formal scheduling makes weak meetings acceptable.

This chapter matters because meetings often receive social protection by default. Once a calendar slot is booked, people treat the time as already justified. That lets poor design hide inside procedure.

The chapter also keeps a necessary limit. Some meetings are useful. Hard tradeoffs, alignment moments, and sensitive conversations can genuinely deserve synchronous time. The goal is not zero meetings. The goal is to make the meeting earn the time it claims. That clears the way for Chapter 16, where the trigger source is no longer a room on the calendar but the device a person carries everywhere.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 15 argues that meetings are attention sinks when they are used as automatic answers to uncertainty, status, or coordination. A meeting is expensive because it converts multiple calendars into one shared claim, often without enough discipline around purpose, scope, or attendance.

Hacking back meetings means treating that claim as something that must be justified. What decision requires live discussion? Who truly needs to attend? What could be handled asynchronously? A meeting becomes much stronger when it has a narrow purpose, fewer people, shorter time, and a real reason to exist.

The chapter's logic is that procedure can hide weak design. A booked room or a scheduled video call often looks legitimate simply because it is formal. The chapter resists that illusion by making meetings answer to cost.

It also avoids the opposite mistake. Some meetings really do help. Difficult tradeoffs, fast alignment, and sensitive conversations can deserve live time. The point is not blanket rejection. The point is earned claim.

That makes the transition to the smartphone useful. After tightening organized workplace claims on attention, the next step is to examine the trigger source that follows a person outside rooms, desks, and schedules.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 15 takes aim at one of office culture's most polished scams: the meeting that steals six calendars and calls the theft teamwork. Once the invite lands, people act like the hour must have been justified by the mere fact that it was reserved.

Eyal's correction is to make meetings earn the time they seize. If the purpose is vague, the agenda is thin, the guest list is swollen, or the issue could have been handled in writing, the meeting is not a solution. It is an attention sink wearing business clothes.

That is why the chapter pushes design discipline. Ask what live decision is actually happening. Cut the room down. Shorten the block. Replace status theater with asynchronous updates. Stop letting formality impersonate necessity.

The chapter stays sane by refusing the lazy anti-meeting rant. Some meetings really do matter. Hard tradeoffs, sensitive issues, and genuine alignment can deserve the room. The point is not to burn the conference table. The point is to stop letting it annex time by default.

That bridge to the smartphone matters because once the organized claims on attention are challenged, the next obvious offender is the portable trigger source people carry into every remaining block of life.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Chapter 15 argues that meetings become distracting when they are allowed to claim shared time by default. A meeting does not merely organize work. It seizes multiple blocks of attention at once, which makes it one of the most expensive routine trigger systems in workplace life.

That is why Eyal treats meetings as claims that must be earned. Purpose matters. Agenda matters. Attendance matters. The possibility of an asynchronous alternative matters. If those elements are weak, the meeting is not neutral. It is a preventable sink for shared attention.

The chapter is especially useful because meetings often hide behind procedure. A booking looks official. A calendar invite looks responsible. A recurring slot looks settled. The chapter breaks that illusion by measuring the meeting against the value it produces rather than the form it takes.

The chapter's answer is design discipline. Narrow the reason for meeting. Tighten the guest list. Shorten the block. Use written updates where live time adds little. Treat synchronous coordination as scarce rather than automatic.

The chapter also resists the lazy anti-meeting posture. Some meetings genuinely deserve the room because real alignment, live tradeoffs, or sensitive issues cannot be handled well in writing. The point is not no meetings. It is fewer unevaluated ones.

That creates a useful bridge to Chapter 16. Once organized group claims on time are challenged, the next trigger source to examine is the personal portable device that keeps generating claims long after the meeting ends.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Chapter 15 says meetings should be understood as costly attention claims, not as neutral scheduling events. Every meeting converts multiple calendars into one synchronous demand, often without sufficient discipline around what the live time is actually buying.

The chapter's central move is to make meetings justify themselves. What decision requires a room? Who truly needs to be present? What part could be handled asynchronously? A meeting earns its claim when the live coordination it creates is worth more than the shared focus it consumes.

This matters because meetings are socially legitimized by form. A recurring invite, a booked conference room, or a video link can make a weak meeting look serious. The chapter rejects that shortcut by treating formality as irrelevant unless purpose is real.

The design response is concrete: tighter agenda, narrower attendance, shorter duration, written alternatives, and resistance to status theater. These are not anti-collaboration moves. They are ways of respecting attention as a scarce shared resource.

The chapter also preserves the right limit. Some meetings should still happen because live alignment, hard tradeoffs, and sensitive conversations do sometimes deserve synchronous time. The goal is not abolition. The goal is earned claim.

That prepares the move to the smartphone well. Once workplace structures stop claiming attention automatically, the next question is how the most portable external-trigger source keeps making its own claims all day.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Chapter 15 goes after a polished form of theft people politely calendar all week: the meeting that hijacks six schedules and expects gratitude because it sent an invite. Once the slot exists, procedure gives the whole thing a halo it may not deserve.

Eyal's answer is simple: make the meeting earn the hour. If the purpose is mushy, the agenda is decorative, the attendee list is bloated, or the same job could be done in writing, then the meeting is not teamwork. It is an attention sink with a conference link.

That matters because meetings hide behind formal respectability. Booked rooms, recurring invites, and video links make weak design look official. The chapter rips away that protection and asks what live coordination is actually being bought.

The fixes are concrete. Cut the room down. Shorten the block. Write the update. Stop staging status theater. Reserve synchronous time for work that genuinely needs human simultaneity.

The chapter also refuses the shallow anti-meeting sermon. Some meetings are worth it. Hard tradeoffs, delicate conversations, and real alignment can deserve the room. The goal is not a scorched-earth calendar. It is to stop giving weak meetings diplomatic immunity.

That bridge to the smartphone matters because once the room loses some of its default power, the next tyrant in line is the device people carry into every remaining corner of the day.
